CHAPTER 1 / WELCOME, RECRUIT
Congratulations on joining Mark Agency, a proud tradition of recovering things other people stole, lost, or insured twice.
This manual is issued by Alex Murphy in the Storage Room. Reading it does not consume it, spend a hint, or deduct money, energy or minutes. Legal insisted we say so in writing. Twice.
If your copy is lost, discarded or eaten, return to Storage. Alex will issue a free replacement, provided you have room in your inventory.
A replacement is not a second recruitment bonus. Please do not apply for a second first day.
The useful bits are always in the back. Ask me how I know.
CHAPTER 2 / DRESS, OPTICS & TRENCH COATS
A detective must look credible to clients and forgettable to suspects. This is achieved with a trench coat. Do not ask how.

items: **Hats:** optional indoors, mandatory in noir.
**Sunglasses:** not indoors, not at night, not ever, according to HR.
**Disguises:** one fake moustache is a disguise. Two is a cry for help.
**Shoes:** quiet ones. Squeaking soles have ended careers.

blocks.text: Agency policy on wigs remains under review since the Lisbon incident.
Wig policy: pending
CHAPTER 3 / STAKEOUTS & SNACK LOGISTICS
A stakeout is waiting, with paperwork. Bring snacks that are silent. Nothing that crunches at the key moment.
Energy matters. A tired detective misses clues and, eventually, the hotel. Sleep and coffee are both resources, but they are not interchangeable, whatever Gordon says.
CHAPTER 4 / INFORMANTS & OTHER UNRELIABLE NARRATORS
Everyone in a city knows something. Most of it is wrong. Some of it is wrong on purpose.

items: A witness who saw everything probably saw nothing.
A witness who saw nothing may be hiding something.
An alibi offered before anyone asks has been rehearsed.
Ask three people. If one lies, it is the one who answers too smoothly.

blocks.text: Chapter 4 is mostly true. The 'mostly' is doing a lot of work.
CHAPTER 5 / EXPENSES, RECEIPTS & THE FINANCE FLOOR
Keep every receipt. Finance does not believe in memory, only in paper.
A taxi ride without a receipt is a gift to the Agency. The Agency has a policy of not accepting gifts, and a second policy of accepting them.
CHAPTER 6 / TELEPHONES, PIGEONS & THE PRESS
Telephones are for asking questions. Pigeons are for questions you do not want overheard. Newspapers tell you tomorrow what everyone knew yesterday.

items: Identify yourself on the phone. Never identify your client.
A pigeon cannot be bugged, but it can be bribed.
The press is not your friend. The press is a friend of the story.

blocks.text: One of the pigeons owes me five.
CHAPTER 7 / CRIME SCENES & THINGS THAT LOOK SUSPICIOUS
At a crime scene everything is evidence until proven otherwise. Then everything is a red herring until proven otherwise. Then it is Tuesday.

items: Look for what does not belong.
Then look for what was meant to look like it does not belong.
Do not touch the alarm. Do not touch the open alarm either. Especially not the open alarm.

blocks.text: A good detective finds three real clues and ignores three decoys. A great detective explains the decoys at dinner.
CHAPTER 8 / LOCKS, SAFES & GORDON
Locks are opened with keys, picks or persuasion. Safes are opened with patience. Gordon's safe is opened with something we are not yet authorised to describe.
Alarm systems: do not trip them. If you trip one, do not look surprised. If surprised, do not run. If running, see Chapter 3 (snacks, quietly).

blocks.title: NOTICE
blocks.text: Safes have dials, pins and regrets. They do not have TEST or MEM buttons. If yours does, it is not a safe.
APPENDIX A / GLOSSARY
**Alibi:** a story with a time stamp.
**Artefact:** expensive, shiny, someone else's.
**Clue:** something helpful, usually found after you needed it.
**Red herring:** a clue that is lying politely.
**Serial number:** the one honest thing about a device. Every device has one. Few advertise it.
**Suspect:** everybody, until Thursday.
APPENDIX B / CARE OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT
Equipment is expensive and sulks. Each device has habits of its own. Rules below apply to the named device only.

head: Device
Procedure
rows: Odd serial: press START. Even serial: press COPY. Nobody knows why.
Odd coins only. Even coins offend it.
It is the 21st century. Why do we have a fax machine?
Press the button once. Pressing it more is a prayer, not a procedure.

blocks.text: APPENDIX C / ETIQUETTE TOWARD ELECTRONICS
Electronic equipment is sensitive and expects to be greeted properly. Do not simply start pressing things. You would not do that at a dinner party. (Do not answer that.)
**First, read the serial number.** It is rarely on the front. Only its final digit matters.

A device whose final digit is **odd** is sociable and expects its greeting from the **MEM** button. A device whose final digit is **even** is formal and expects the **TEST** button. Zero counts as even. Zero is also what you will score if you guess.
This applies to devices that have both buttons. Kettles are exempt.
Greeting is not leaving. Leaving is in the back, the sad part.
APPENDIX D / FAREWELLS
Whatever the device asked of you in between (manufacturers love their own paperwork, so consult it), every visit ends the same way.

items: Press the OTHER greeting button, the one you did not open with. Equipment keeps score.
Press **ENTER**. Once. Firmly. It is not a lift.

blocks.text: Only then may you consider the device settled. Do not thank it. It will not reply, and it will remember.
APPENDIX E / APPROVED EXCUSES FOR BEING IN A MUSEUM AFTER HOURS

items: **I was looking for the toilets.** Accepted once. Do not reuse.
**I am from the Ministry of Inspection.** Which ministry? Be ready.
**I fell asleep.** Believable. Embarrassing.
**I am with the pigeons.** Nobody will ask a second question.
